article.heading: Converting schemas without losing the assumptions
article.p1: A database table and a Java class describe different things. SQL records storage rules, constraints, indexes and expressions. A Java model describes values and application behaviour. This converter introduces an intermediate schema so you can inspect both views before downloading files. Start by choosing PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server or SQLite, paste one or more CREATE TABLE statements, and select the desired output. The tool parses SQL into an abstract syntax tree. It never executes statements or connects to a database. An unsupported statement blocks export rather than disappearing silently.
article.p2: Entity output includes persistence annotations and requires a primary key. Composite keys use IdClass with an equality implementation. Foreign keys remain scalar values, avoiding accidental relationship loading. DTO classes contain no persistence annotations; request and response variants let you exclude identifiers, audit fields and sensitive fields. Partial UpdateRequest output does not inherit required-field validation. Records require Java 16 or later. Interface projections expose getters and need property names or SQL aliases that Spring Data can resolve. Simple SELECT expressions without known types are explicitly marked for review.
article.p3: For reverse conversion, paste a field-based Java class or a record. The supported Java declaration parser reads scalar fields and common JPA column annotations, skips method bodies, and rejects inheritance, generics and relationship declarations it cannot faithfully interpret. Review the mapping table before generating SQL: a missing length is not secretly replaced with VARCHAR(255), and a field named id is not automatically considered generated. Unknown nullability remains visible. The database draft therefore captures your chosen assumptions, not a promise to recreate a lost production schema.
article.p4: Choose the Spring Boot namespace, Java version, package, constructors, validation and naming options in the advanced panel. Individual files can be copied or downloaded, and ZIP export preserves package folders plus the intermediate metadata. Keep that sidecar when reviewing cross-dialect output, because defaults and provider-specific types may need manual migration work. SQL and Java stay in the browser, processing runs in a worker with a time limit, and no credentials are requested. Review all warnings and test the generated code with your actual dependencies before adopting it.

faq.heading: Questions
faq.a1: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB (common MySQL-compatible DDL), SQL Server and SQLite within the documented subset. Oracle is not supported yet.
faq.q2: Does Java → SQL recover the exact schema?
faq.a2: No. DTOs and records lack database metadata; review and supply the missing information before using the draft.
faq.q3: Is any code uploaded or executed?
faq.a3: No. Parsing and generation run locally. SQL and input Java are never executed.
